title: Vy, or ty?
situation: Your office has a mix of formal and first-name relationships. Knowing who gets vy, who gets ty and when to switch is a social skill as much as grammar.

canDo.text: You can choose vy or ty for the person in front of you.
You can ask simple questions in both the vy and the ty form.
You can recognise the offer to switch to ty, and accept it.

missions.title: Notice the switch
missions.task: Listen out at work this week: who says ty to whom, and who says vy? If someone offers ty (Můžeme si tykat?), accept it the Czech way.
missions.ifStuck: Když nevíš, vykej. When in doubt, say vy: nobody minds being treated politely.

exercises.prompt: A police officer asks for your ID. **vy** or **ty**?

hints.explain: A police officer is a stranger doing their job: always vy.

exercises.why: A police officer is a stranger doing their job: always vy.

exercises.prompt: Your neighbour's ten-year-old son says hello. **vy** or **ty**?

hints.explain: Children get ty from everyone, neighbours included.

exercises.why: With vy the verb is 2nd person plural, even to one person: Kde bydlíte?

hints.explain: Bydlíš is the ty form. To a neighbour you say vy to: bydlíte.

exercises.prompt: Kde ___? (to Ondra, a colleague you say ty to)
exercises.why: Friends get ty, so the verb is 2nd person singular: Kde bydlíš?

hints.explain: Bydlíte is the vy form. With Ondra you say ty: bydlíš.

context.speaker: Petra
context.cs: Můžeme si tykat? Já jsem Petra.
context.en: Shall we say ty? I'm Petra.

exercises.prompt: Accept, as a man, and say your name is Tom.
exercises.why: To accept, say yes (jasně, rád / ráda) and give your first name.

hints.explain: Ráda is the feminine form. A man says rád.
